title: Certificate Authority
summary: A certificate authority is the trusted entity that verifies the identity behind a public key and signs a certificate binding that identity to the key, which is what lets a client trust a server it has never met before. In the web public key infrastructure, a root authority holds a self-signed root certificate that ships inside operating systems and browsers, and it normally issues through intermediate authorities so the root key can stay offline; those roots and intermediates form a chain of trust that a validating client walks from the server certificate up to a trust anchor. Validation covers far more than a signature: the client checks the certificate is inside its validity dates, that the name matches the site being reached, that each issuer was permitted to issue for that purpose, and that the certificate has not been revoked. Because every major client trusts a large set of roots, the practical risk concentrates on operations rather than mathematics: a weak domain validation process can let someone obtain a certificate for a domain they do not control, and a stolen or misused issuing key can produce trusted certificates at scale. The common mistake is to assume that a padlock means the site is honest, when it only means the name was validated by some authority the browser trusts at that moment.

beginner.definition: A certificate authority is a trusted organisation that proves a website is really who it claims to be. It checks the details and then signs a digital certificate. Browsers keep a list of authorities they trust. If a site shows a valid certificate from that list, your browser accepts the connection.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without this check, anyone could pretend to be your bank and read your data. A certificate also makes the connection private, so others cannot read it. If an authority checks badly, an attacker can get a valid certificate for a site they do not own. The browser would then show a padlock on a fake site. Careful checking is what keeps trust meaningful.
howItWorks: A website creates a key pair and keeps the private key secret on its server.
The site sends a request with its name and public key to a certificate authority.
The authority then proves that the requester really controls that domain name.
The authority signs a certificate that links the domain name to that public key.
Your browser checks the signature, the dates, and the name before it connects.
Browsers also check a published list to see revoked certificates are refused.
beginner.example: Think of a passport office. You prove who you are with documents, and the office issues a passport that other countries accept. A border guard trusts the passport because the issuing office is known and the stamp is hard to copy. If the office handed passports to anyone who asked, every border would become unsafe. The whole system rests on careful checking.
takeaways: A padlock means the name was checked by a trusted authority, not that the site is honest.
Protect the private key of a certificate, because a copy lets others impersonate you.
Watch your certificates before they expire, since an expired one breaks the site.

objectives: Explain what a certificate authority does and the trust problem it solves.
Describe the chain of trust from a server certificate to a trusted root.
List the checks a client performs before accepting a certificate.
Explain why domain validation quality matters as much as the cryptography.
Describe what can go wrong when an issuing key is stolen or misused.
Explain the role of revocation and how it affects a live connection.
